0. How to use this GDD

This is the canonical full game-design document for Probably Paradise. Use it with:

  • DOCS/PROBABLY_PARADISE_GAME_VISION.md for the creative north star and direction states;
  • DESIGN/PLAYABLE_DESIGN.md for the active mechanics prototype;
  • DESIGN/GAMEPLAY_LOOP.md for the implementation-neutral inner/outer loop diagram;
  • DESIGN/CHARACTER_ART_DIRECTION.md for character/art constraints;
  • DESIGN/DECISION_LOG.md for accepted supersession and governance decisions;
  • DESIGN/OPEN_QUESTIONS.md for unresolved product questions.

Pair a Dice GDD material under FOUNDATION/ is historical/superseded. It remains useful evidence for the origin and mechanics of the project, but its fixed-island and pixel-art directions are not current.

0.1 Direction states

  • Accepted / Strong Direction: protect the product principle; implementation details may still need refinement.
  • Promising Territory: investigate with bounded evidence before making it a requirement.
  • Open: no accepted answer; agents must not decide it silently.
  • Historical / Superseded: truthful prior authority that no longer directs current work.

Examples are not requirements unless a current accepted card explicitly makes them so.

0.2 Product authority

  1. Explicit owner instruction.
  2. Accepted decisions in DESIGN/DECISION_LOG.md.
  3. Active DESIGN/PLAYABLE_DESIGN.md for the prototype.
  4. This GDD and the canonical Game Vision.
  5. Accepted experiment evidence.
  6. Current Ready work card.
  7. Technical architecture and official Godot guidance for engine behavior.
  8. Existing implementation as current-state evidence.

Implementation never becomes product authority merely because it exists.

01

1. Product summary

1.1 High concept — Strong Direction

STRONG

Probably Paradise is a hand-drawn surreal comedic roguelite about two well-worn polyhedral dice who fall out of an ordinary tabletop game and begin an impossible journey toward something they believe is Paradise. They use a crude travel journal, reason competently from a worldview built out of games about reality, and accumulate evidence that changes what the player and dice recognize across runs.

1.2 Player promise — Strong Direction

STRONG

The player should feel:

  • clever for finding a useful interpretation of an uncertain roll;
  • responsible for manipulating and committing the active pair;
  • curious about unfamiliar worlds, unknown entries, and future combinations;
  • attached to different dice and the relationships they form;
  • surprised when prior context changes a later run;
  • able to understand authoritative results even when the fictional journal is wrong;
  • motivated by “one more run because I want to see what happens.”

1.3 Primary differentiator — Strong Direction

STRONG

Two active heterogeneous polyhedral dice whose relationship becomes the build.

The pair matters more than either die alone.

The game is not simply a roguelite that uses dice as generic resources. Die geometry, face range, distribution, relative results, manipulation, character context, and pair relationship must matter.

1.4 Retention fantasy — Strong Direction

STRONG

The player understands the grammar of the game but not the next combination. Curiosity produces memory, recognition, and connection rather than a manipulative reward schedule. The journal makes unknowns visible and lets earlier evidence matter later.

02

2. Design pillars

Pillar A — The pair is the build

Meaningful decisions should depend on the relationship between the two active dice. A feature that works identically with generic cards or six-sided dice is underusing the premise.

Pillar B — Luck creates a problem; the player plays with it

Randomness establishes the situation. Readable manipulation, commitment, routes, and build context create agency. Bad rolls may create difficult decisions, but should not routinely prevent meaningful play from beginning.

Pillar C — Every run leaves evidence

Failure may prevent advancement toward Paradise without erasing discovery. Evidence is not automatically currency, stats, loot, or consolation power.

Pillar D — Curiosity is rewarded with memory

World, journal, character, pair, bench, run, visual, and belief contexts can contribute to recognition and callbacks. These contexts must not automatically become separate engineered systems.

Pillar E — The dice are competent within the wrong frame

Comedy comes from capable reasoning applied to incomplete or misapplied premises, not from calling the protagonists idiots.

Pillar F — Absurdity follows rules

Escalation, association, recurrence, sincerity, silence, and specificity create comedy. Disconnected randomness and imitation do not.

Pillar G — Fiction may be unreliable; state may not

The journal can contradict itself, misclassify evidence, and express impossible confidence. Authoritative gameplay/save state must remain deterministic, inspectable, and correct.

Pillar H — Readability before decoration

The player must quickly identify die type, result, state, emotion, and relationship. Handmade presentation cannot obscure mechanics.

03

3. Cast and narrative premise

3.1 Cast — Strong Direction

STRONG
  • d4
  • d6
  • d8
  • d10
  • d%
  • d12
  • d20

The die is the body. Native geometry, movement, mechanics, expression, behavior, dialogue, journal edits, history, and pair context create character. Exact personalities are Open.

Seven dice create 21 possible two-die pair relationships before other context is added.

3.2 Origin in the fiction — Strong Direction

STRONG

The dice are experienced communal tabletop objects, not magical chosen heroes. They have absorbed fragments from rulebooks, boards, cards, miniatures, flavor text, campaigns, conversations, disputes, celebrations, accusations, and repairs. They mistake experience with games about reality for experience with reality itself.

3.3 Inciting incident — Strong Direction

STRONG

Two dice tumble out of an ordinary tabletop game. What is a minor dropped-piece accident to humans becomes an impossible journey for the dice. Human faces and biographies are unnecessary; hands, shadows, sleeves, table clutter, and game components can establish scale.

3.4 Paradise — Open

OPEN

Paradise is the destination or concept the dice pursue. Its objective nature, final meaning, ending relationship, and whether it is a place at all remain Open. It is not canonically a fixed tropical island or a biblical afterlife.

3.5 Personal Truth boundary — Accepted governance

ACCEPTED

Personal Truth may only originate from the owner.

Agents, skills, models, generators, and automated systems may never manufacture memories, family stories, private jokes, emotional meaning, personal experiences, or biographical provenance. They may work with such material only after the owner supplies it.

If a design moment would benefit from authentic personal context, an agent may invite the owner to provide a relevant memory or experience, but it must not assume one exists, invent details, pressure the owner to disclose anything, or treat disclosure as required.

Private creative provenance is never exposed automatically. Public fictional material must work without private context and follow DOCS/PRIVATE_PROVENANCE_POLICY.md.

04

4. Core gameplay model

4.1 Active pair — Strong Direction

STRONG

Standard resolution uses exactly two active dice. Additional owned, inactive, reserve, or temporary dice are Open and must not weaken pair identity.

4.2 Data-driven dice — Strong Direction

STRONG

A die definition must not assume six faces. It may eventually include:

  • stable ID;
  • display name;
  • ordered face definitions or face count;
  • tags or properties;
  • mechanical traits only after accepted design evidence;
  • presentation references separate from canonical rules.

Standard cast geometry does not restrict the engine to a hard-coded list.

4.3 Gameplay thesis — Strong Direction at principle level

STRONG

The player solves changing situations by making the best possible use of an imperfect pair.

The active pair determines the immediate possibility space. Die History modifies how that pair behaves. The current world changes which relationships and outcomes matter. The roll creates constraints and opportunities. The player manipulates and commits those results to a solution. The consequence creates evidence, and the journal carries useful, disputed, or incomplete knowledge forward.

Choose the pair. Roll the problem. Make the best of it. Remember what happened.

This is a hypothesis to prototype. It does not establish combat, dungeon crawling, card battling, or another familiar genre as the final game.

4.3.1 Inner loop — situation solving

SITUATION → READ → ROLL → MANIPULATE → COMMIT → RESOLVE → LEARN

  1. Situation: a visible problem, opportunity, threat, obstacle, conversation, escape, or discovery establishes what matters.
  2. Read: the player sees the relevant Pair, History, World Rule, Journal knowledge, constraints, and likely consequences.
  3. Roll: explicit seeded RNG produces one valid result for each active die.
  4. Manipulate: the player uses bounded, transparent control to work with the problem.
  5. Commit: the player accepts and assigns the current results to a solution.
  6. Resolve: deterministic rules produce readable outcome data and consequences.
  7. Learn: the outcome may create evidence, change a belief, expose an unknown, or leave the situation unresolved.

The narrower post-situation grammar remains useful inside the loop:

ROLL → READ → MANIPULATE → COMMIT → RESOLVE

The exact manipulation vocabulary is Open / Prototype Territory. Reroll, rotate, ±1, bank, swap, sacrifice, exhaust, and overdrive are candidate verbs, not accepted final mechanics. The future Mechanics Lab contract is specified in DESIGN/PLAYABLE_DESIGN.md; its target, budget, score values, relationships, and verbs remain experimental variables.

4.3.2 Outer loop — journey and memory

CHOOSE / FORM PAIR → JOURNEY → SITUATIONS → CONSEQUENCES → JOURNAL / MEMORY CHANGES → FUTURE RUN CONTEXT → GO AGAIN

The outer loop can create pair selection or change, impossible worlds, situations, History, discoveries, journal evidence, corrected or disputed beliefs, fake-tabletop echoes, bench memory, callbacks, Paradise theories, and changes in future possibility. Exact persistence and progression systems remain Open or Promising Territory.

Inner-loop decisions create evidence that changes the outer loop, and outer-loop memory changes what the player can recognize or meaningfully attempt in future inner-loop situations.

4.3.3 Four sources of situation specificity — Prototype hypothesis

PROTOTYPE
  • Pair — What can I currently do? Active dice, geometry, face ranges, distributions, and relationship define the immediate possibility space.
  • History — What is unusual about these particular dice? Prior events may change how a die behaves or how the pair is evaluated.
  • World Rule — What matters here? An environment may change which values, relationships, geometries, actions, costs, or information matter.
  • Journal — What do I already know, suspect, misunderstand, or remember? Knowledge may expose options, warnings, unknowns, failed attempts, disputed facts, or patterns.

Use manipulation and commitment to reconcile the Pair, History, World Rule, and Journal knowledge presented by the current situation.

This model is not proof of a final implementation.

4.4 Relationship engine — Strong Direction

STRONG

The resolver may derive only what current mechanics need from:

  • equality or matching;
  • absolute difference and distance thresholds;
  • sum;
  • parity;
  • relative order;
  • minimum/maximum relative to each die;
  • percentile-relative positions across different die sizes;
  • accepted tags or traits in later work.

Current prototype relationships remain Match, Close, Far, Odd Couple, and Extremes. They exist to test distinct reasons to value different pairs, not to establish a final content catalog.

4.5 Manipulation — Strong Direction with Open implementation

STRONGOPEN

Manipulation must create agency, have explicit limits, remain deterministic, and show its consequences. A future laboratory may test rerolling one die, rotating a result by ±1, or another minimal bounded set, but no specific verb is canonized before evidence. The final manipulation vocabulary and economy are Open.

4.6 Transparent resolution — Strong Direction

STRONG

Authoritative results must provide a readable breakdown. UI renders result data; it does not own or invent gameplay rules. Animation callbacks never decide outcomes.

4.7 History and role guardrails — Promising Territory

PROMISING

What happened to a die before this journey can change how that die behaves now.

Illustrative History families include Rolled, Thrown, Borrowed, Dropped, Blamed, Celebrated, Cursed, and Lost. A useful History Trait should communicate a specific past, alter evaluation of the current pair, and create a tradeoff, condition, rule interaction, or changed decision rather than generic numerical inflation.

If the flavor or name can be removed and the mechanic becomes indistinguishable from a generic stat modifier, the History Trait probably needs further design work.

History should normally change how fair outcomes are interpreted or used rather than secretly changing a physical die's probability distribution. A d8 should normally remain an honest d8; exceptions require explicit justification.

A modifier can change meaning because the pair changes.

A Blamed condition that cares about rolling below the partner would behave differently across pairs. History should perturb and deepen pair composition rather than replace it.

Research labels such as Spark, Guard, Control, Strike, Fate, Power, and Chaos are exploratory scaffolding, not canonical classes or permanent die roles. Protect instead:

Geometry creates tendencies. History creates quirks. Pairing creates capabilities. World creates context.

The d4 may be the hero, liability, only shape that fits, a Blamed die seeking a d20 partner, or the die carrying questionable EXTREME GRANDMA knowledge. No die collapses into one class.

4.8 Depth target — Unvalidated

PROTOTYPE

Probably Paradise does not claim Balatro-level depth. Depth should emerge from interacting systems rather than a huge catalog of isolated bonuses.

Candidate combinatorial structure:

PAIR × HISTORY × WORLD RULE × SITUATION × ROLL × MANIPULATION × JOURNAL KNOWLEDGE

Prototype whether these dimensions meaningfully multiply one another. Do not respond to insufficient depth by authoring hundreds of modifiers.

05

5. Encounters and worlds

5.1 Situation grammar — Promising Territory

PROMISING

A situation may be expressed as a visible problem or opportunity, ruleset, objective, pressure, environmental rule, available information, optional discovery, and consequence. Combat is one candidate situation type, not the default genre. Traversal, escape, survival, negotiation, investigation, opportunity, puzzle-like constraints, environmental interaction, absurd rule-following, and discovery should be able to test the same dice grammar. Creatures, travelers, institutions, obstacles, hazards, misunderstandings, games, and self-created problems can all establish situations.

5.2 Impossible-world structure — Strong Direction

STRONG

The journey is not island-bound. Associative transitions can connect radically different conceptual environments while the cast and journal preserve coherence.

Every accepted world should eventually earn its place through:

  1. a visual premise;
  2. a comedic premise;
  3. an environmental rule;
  4. something the dice misunderstand;
  5. a journal consequence.

Whether the environmental rule changes dice mechanics is Promising Territory.

World Rules should eventually justify more than art or background changes. They may change which results matter, pair interpretation, exact totals or relationships, geometry advantages, manipulation costs, available information, or possible actions. Whale-subway exact fare, microscopic scale rewarding smaller geometry, giant scale changing size relevance, zero gravity reinterpreting high/low, and bureaucracy imposing ridiculous eligibility constraints are waystones only.

5.3 Lodestones and waystones

ILLUSTRATIVE

Lodestones are durable principles. Waystones are illustrative possibilities.

TABLE → FLOOR → BASEMENT → SEWER → OCEAN → ABYSS → WHALE → SPACE → ??? → PARADISE is a waystone, not a campaign order or biome requirement.

5.4 World topology — Open

OPEN

Do not default to a conventional branching node map merely because it is familiar. A journal route/map surface is Strong Direction; the exact topology, route rules, world order, and campaign structure remain Open.

06

6. Journal, knowledge, and progression

6.1 Journal role — Strong Direction

STRONG

The journal is a heavily used, badly drawn notebook that can combine route/map, run evidence, discoveries, unknowns, character voice, pair context, tutorials, theories, recurring motifs, and long-term recognition.

6.2 Documented Facts — Strong Direction

STRONG

Documented Facts are character-authored conclusions, not omniscient developer truth. They can be disputed, corrected, contradicted, or supported later. The underlying state must remain reliable.

6.3 Unknown knowledge — Strong Direction

STRONG

Silhouettes, sketches, ???, rumors, partial descriptions, disputed classifications, and unreliable sources make mystery visible before it is understood. Additional evidence may reduce or worsen fictional confidence.

6.4 Characterization through edits — Strong Direction

STRONG

Handwriting, corrections, doodles, underlines, marginalia, arguments, and crossed-out corrections can express personality and remembered context without constant dialogue.

6.5 Run persistence — Strong Direction at principle level

STRONG

Every run leaves evidence. At minimum, prior play can influence what the journal or future cold open recognizes. The data model and persistence mechanics remain unimplemented and require later refined work.

Journal knowledge may eventually change future decision space rather than merely unlock flavor. Meta-progression through knowledge could make situations more legible without conventional permanent-stat inflation; exact representation and effect remain Promising Territory.

6.6 Progression — Open / Promising Territory

PROMISINGOPEN

Long-term progression should increase curiosity, knowledge, route understanding, pair context, and recognition rather than defaulting to raw permanent power. Exact unlocks, mechanical persistence, history traits, bench memory, economy, and collection structure remain Open or Promising Territory.

6.7 Failure — Open

OPEN

Failure must create stakes without routinely denying meaningful play. A failed run may still leave discovery. The run-ending model, encounter-local consequences, attrition, time pressure, and hybrid options remain Open.

6.8 Mechanical-memory waystones — Illustrative only

ILLUSTRATIVE

These examples show mechanics, character, memory, comedy, and journal knowledge affecting the same decision. They are not required shipping encounters, Traits, or systems.

Exact fare / Blamed / trains:

The player needs d4 to remain below d12 so Blamed triggers, but also needs the pair total to equal 11 because a whale subway requires exact fare.

d4 may insist, “This is how trains work,” because it was used several runs earlier in EXTREME GRANDMA. The journal might record TRAINS, exact fare, frequent Grandma destinations, and Confidence: HIGH.

Suspicious Hole: an entry can move from ???, through a failed d12 attempt and disputed POWER, toward SMALL SHAPE and eventually d4 ✓. The point is future legibility, not a locked knowledge mechanic.

Rules Lawyer: d8's time in WHALE LAWYER might later make a written rule challengeable. This illustrates:

FAKE GAME → BENCH MEMORY → DIE BELIEF / HISTORY → FUTURE SITUATION OPTION → CONSEQUENCE → JOURNAL

Memories may seed one another conceptually. This does not authorize memory architecture.

07

7. Fake tabletop cold opens

7.1 Cold-open identity — Strong Direction

STRONG

Each run can begin inside a crude fictional tabletop game. The opening reinforces the dice's worldview and the ordinary scale of the initiating tabletop.

7.2 Memory echoes — Strong Direction / Promising Territory

STRONGPROMISING

The cold open can remember previous play and turn it into new fictional context. A visual echo is the safest first expression. Journal echoes are central. Mechanical echoes and generated/assembled fake-game corpora remain Promising Territory.

Examples are waystones, not a required content list.

08

8. Character and art direction

8.1 Active style — Strong Direction

STRONG

Crude-but-confident hand-drawn digital illustration is the active direction. Use handmade imperfection, strong readability, thick uneven outlines, simple flat color, sparse scribbled shading, expressive silhouette, limited animation, pose changes, reaction timing, paper/tape/cardboard/index-card UI, and controlled visual jokes.

Pixel art is not the default. Avoid generic polished fantasy, generic cozy presentation, glossy mobile rendering, polished vector mascots, high-detail 3D, and direct imitation.

8.2 Native geometry — Strong Direction

STRONG

The d4, d6, d8, d10, d%, d12, and d20 must remain recognizable from silhouette and face structure. The die remains the dominant mass. Character additions remain minimal, removable for mechanical clarity, and cheap enough to reproduce consistently.

8.3 Dual-state hypothesis — Promising Territory

PROMISINGPROTOTYPE

The strongest current presentation hypothesis lets a die move between character state and clean game-piece/roll state. Prototype it against literal living dice and separate commentary-companion presentations before locking the final model.

8.4 Pair-driven characterization — Strong Direction

STRONG

Character design includes who a die becomes with each partner. Mechanical synergy, conflict, risk, history, and shared context can affect behavior. Avoid seven static sitcom archetypes.

8.5 Originality — Accepted boundary

ACCEPTED

Influences provide principles, not assets, style-transfer prompts, constructions, voices, jokes, brands, or copied content. Use DOCS/PROBABLY_PARADISE_GAME_VISION.md for the canonical influence list and anti-imitation rule.

09

9. Interface and accessibility

9.1 Information hierarchy — Strong Direction

STRONG

The player should quickly answer:

  • What am I trying to do?
  • What are the two active dice?
  • What did each roll?
  • Which relationship matters and why?
  • What can I manipulate?
  • What will happen if I commit?
  • What is reliable state versus character-authored belief?

9.2 Journal UI — Strong Direction / Open implementation

STRONGOPEN

The journal should feel used, revised, and character-authored while system text remains readable. Handmade treatment cannot sacrifice accessibility or authoritative state clarity.

9.3 Accessibility — Strong Direction

STRONG
  • no mechanic communicated only by color;
  • scalable and readable text;
  • keyboard and mouse support on Windows;
  • controller-compatible architecture when relevant;
  • reduced motion and fast/skip resolution paths;
  • readable numeric outcomes and breakdowns;
  • no unapproved timed pressure;
  • focus, hover, disabled, and error states when interactions exist.
10

10. Audio direction

10.1 Strong Direction

STRONG

Audio should feel authored and tactile: dice clacks, table knocks, paper, marker, cardboard, plastic pieces, and deliberately contrasted musical or Foley choices can support the handmade universe.

10.2 Open

OPEN

Final genre, instrumentation, voice treatment, world-specific score systems, and production pipeline are unresolved. World hopping permits contrast; it does not require a large soundtrack before the gameplay is proven.

11

11. Technical design constraints

11.1 Baseline — Accepted

ACCEPTED
  • Godot 4.7.2 stable, verified build 4.7.2.stable.official.ed1daf0bf;
  • GDScript;
  • Windows PC first;
  • Godot project root GAME/;
  • feature-oriented organization;
  • Git and governed SQLite operational memory.

11.2 Domain boundaries — Strong Direction

STRONG

Prefer:

input intent → validation → domain transition → deterministic outcome → presentation

Keep dice definitions separate from visuals, RNG results separate from animation, relationships/scoring separate from labels/effects, authored data separate from debug output, and authoritative save state separate from the fictional journal's claims.

11.3 Deterministic RNG — Strong Direction

STRONG

Gameplay randomness must use explicit seed ownership and reproducible state. Do not scatter uncontrolled random calls through scenes.

11.4 Data and IDs — Strong Direction

STRONG

Prefer stable IDs and data-driven definitions. Do not hard-code six faces. Preserve enough seed, pair, encounter, and action context to reproduce defects.

11.5 Memory compatibility — Requirement, not architecture

ACCEPTED

Future state must be capable of distinguishing objective world/save facts from journal beliefs and of representing relevant run, character, and pair context if later cards accept those mechanics. PP-002 does not choose tables, Resources, services, schemas, save formats, or event systems for that future.

11.6 Architecture anti-goals

Avoid speculative factories, service locators, universal event buses, giant autoloads, generic managers, premature content pipelines, and separate systems for every named memory category.

12

12. QA strategy

12.1 Automated proof

Use focused deterministic checks for:

  • valid faces and no d6 assumption;
  • reproducible seeded rolls;
  • deterministic relationship predicates;
  • score/effect breakdown equality;
  • valid IDs/references;
  • state/presentation agreement;
  • saved authoritative state when persistence exists.

Exhaust small N×M ordered outcome spaces when directly relevant. Even d20+d20 has only 400 base outcomes.

12.2 Rendered proof

Player-visible changes require the real Godot scene: controls, states, readability, scaling, focus/hover/disabled behavior, animation synchronization, and debugger/output inspection.

12.3 Human judgment

Automated tests and RobQA do not prove fun, desired balance, art taste, or emotional payoff. Owner/playtest evidence decides those questions.

13

13. Prototype and production program

Gate 0 — Foundation

Repository, operational memory, Godot project, minimal boot scene, headless validation, and owner-rendered foundation. PAD-000/PAD-001 are historical work; PP-002 migrates their active context without rewriting history.

Gate 1 — Mechanics Lab

The next experiment should test whether choosing and operating exactly two heterogeneous dice creates interesting decisions while solving changing situations under uncertainty. Build only a future owner-authorized playable-design scope and proportional tests. Do not build full narrative, production journal mechanics, world map, production art, economy, or meta progression.

Decision questions:

Is choosing and operating a heterogeneous pair of polyhedral dice fun when solving changing situations under uncertainty?

Can Pair + History + World Rule + manipulation create interesting decisions without relying solely on combat?

A minimal future laboratory may compare threat, obstacle/traversal, and opportunity/discovery situations. PP-002 does not start or implement that laboratory.

Gate 2 — Micro Run

Only after Gate 1 acceptance, test whether reward choices and a short encounter sequence create build development and another-run pull. Failure and progression require explicit owner decisions.

Gate 3 — Probably Paradise vertical slice

Only after prior gates, prove the creative fantasy with a representative impossible journey, character/art direction, central journal surface, audio, accessibility, persistence appropriate to accepted design, and a small set of encounters.

Gate 4 — Production

Only after vertical-slice acceptance set production content budget, demo/Steam strategy, full platform plan, and marketing/community scope.

14

14. Scope guardrails

Before Mechanics Lab acceptance, do not build:

  • production world topology or large encounter libraries;
  • journal, Confidence, History Trait, bench-memory, or fake-game systems;
  • large story/dialogue, shops, economy, crafting, or meta progression;
  • production art/audio libraries or elaborate animation;
  • save systems beyond accepted debug/reproduction needs;
  • Steam, achievements, multiplayer, ports, accounts, or online services;
  • elaborate procedural generation or speculative frameworks.

Before vertical-slice acceptance, do not build full campaign content, final economy, large persistent progression, extensive lore databases, modding, or release-scale systems.

15

15. Promising Territory summary

  • Confidence and evolving Paradise theories;
  • History Traits and die-specific pasts;
  • world rules affecting pair decisions;
  • fake-game generation or assembly;
  • bench lives and memory;
  • pair-context dialogue and arguments;
  • journal divergence and correction;
  • cross-seeding among memory contexts;
  • informational rarity and unknown taxonomy;
  • journal-led route/map interface;
  • mechanical echoes between runs;
  • dual-state character/game-piece presentation.

These require evidence, not implementation enthusiasm.

16

16. Open Questions summary

  • objective nature of Paradise and ending structure;
  • final commercially cleared title;
  • exact seven personalities;
  • final character/game-piece presentation model;
  • failure and pressure model;
  • manipulation limits and economy;
  • dice replacement, swapping, and reserve rules;
  • world topology and progression;
  • Confidence implementation;
  • History Trait ownership and persistence;
  • bench and pair-memory mechanics;
  • journal belief divergence;
  • fake-game authoring method;
  • Documented Facts mechanics;
  • long-term progression;
  • run length, content budget, and release strategy.

Open questions are not technical debt.

17

17. Success and failure signals

Success signals

Players talk about:

  • the specific pair they used;
  • a roll they manipulated into a meaningful commitment;
  • a relationship or geometry interaction they understood;
  • a strange discovery or unknown they want to revisit;
  • the journal remembering, disputing, or revising something;
  • a callback whose prior context they recognize;
  • caring whether the dice find Paradise;
  • choosing another run to see what happens.

Failure signals

  • the largest die is always best;
  • rerolling the lower number is always correct;
  • relationships are incidental;
  • manipulation is cosmetic or luck routinely removes agency;
  • dice could be swapped for generic resources without loss;
  • the journal is optional lore rather than central;
  • worlds are disconnected random jokes or conventional biome filler;
  • the game defaults back to fixed islands or generic pixel art;
  • fictional unreliability corrupts authoritative state;
  • references become imitation;
  • private provenance appears in a public or player-facing surface.
18

18. Provenance and supersession

This GDD synthesizes the public-safe canonical Game Vision, active character-driven art specification, still-valid pair mechanics from the historical Pair a Dice GDD and active Playable Design, structural lessons from the supplied GDD references, accepted project decisions, and the PP-002 governing contract.

It does not retroactively rename Pair a Dice history. It supersedes the historical full GDD only for current product authority.

RESEARCH/PROBABLY_PARADISE_POLYHEDRAL_DICE_MECHANICS_RESEARCH.md remains non-binding research evidence. Its probability differences, exact-face/event frequencies, mismatched-pair distributions, and pre/post-roll/across-turn agency concepts may inform experiments. Its recommended genre, temporary role labels, reserve/third-die systems, and other scaffolding do not become authority automatically. The canonical cast excludes d2 regardless of any research or historical example.

Research informs design. Owner-accepted authority governs design.

# Probably Paradise — Game Design Document

**Working identity/title candidate:** Probably Paradise  
**Commercial-name status:** Clearance required before commercial commitment  
**Document status:** Canonical living GDD  
**Authority state:** Active under PP-002  
**Engine:** Godot 4.7.2 stable  
**Language:** GDScript  
**Primary platform:** Windows PC first  
**Design maturity:** Preproduction; Strong Direction, Promising Territory, and Open Questions remain distinct

## 0. How to use this GDD

This is the canonical full game-design document for Probably Paradise. Use it with:

- `DOCS/PROBABLY_PARADISE_GAME_VISION.md` for the creative north star and direction states;
- `DESIGN/PLAYABLE_DESIGN.md` for the active mechanics prototype;
- `DESIGN/GAMEPLAY_LOOP.md` for the implementation-neutral inner/outer loop diagram;
- `DESIGN/CHARACTER_ART_DIRECTION.md` for character/art constraints;
- `DESIGN/DECISION_LOG.md` for accepted supersession and governance decisions;
- `DESIGN/OPEN_QUESTIONS.md` for unresolved product questions.

Pair a Dice GDD material under `FOUNDATION/` is historical/superseded. It remains useful evidence for the origin and mechanics of the project, but its fixed-island and pixel-art directions are not current.

### 0.1 Direction states

- **Accepted / Strong Direction:** protect the product principle; implementation details may still need refinement.
- **Promising Territory:** investigate with bounded evidence before making it a requirement.
- **Open:** no accepted answer; agents must not decide it silently.
- **Historical / Superseded:** truthful prior authority that no longer directs current work.

Examples are not requirements unless a current accepted card explicitly makes them so.

### 0.2 Product authority

1. Explicit owner instruction.
2. Accepted decisions in `DESIGN/DECISION_LOG.md`.
3. Active `DESIGN/PLAYABLE_DESIGN.md` for the prototype.
4. This GDD and the canonical Game Vision.
5. Accepted experiment evidence.
6. Current Ready work card.
7. Technical architecture and official Godot guidance for engine behavior.
8. Existing implementation as current-state evidence.

Implementation never becomes product authority merely because it exists.

## 1. Product summary

### 1.1 High concept — Strong Direction

Probably Paradise is a hand-drawn surreal comedic roguelite about two well-worn polyhedral dice who fall out of an ordinary tabletop game and begin an impossible journey toward something they believe is Paradise. They use a crude travel journal, reason competently from a worldview built out of games about reality, and accumulate evidence that changes what the player and dice recognize across runs.

### 1.2 Player promise — Strong Direction

The player should feel:

- clever for finding a useful interpretation of an uncertain roll;
- responsible for manipulating and committing the active pair;
- curious about unfamiliar worlds, unknown entries, and future combinations;
- attached to different dice and the relationships they form;
- surprised when prior context changes a later run;
- able to understand authoritative results even when the fictional journal is wrong;
- motivated by “one more run because I want to see what happens.”

### 1.3 Primary differentiator — Strong Direction

> **Two active heterogeneous polyhedral dice whose relationship becomes the build.**

> **The pair matters more than either die alone.**

The game is not simply a roguelite that uses dice as generic resources. Die geometry, face range, distribution, relative results, manipulation, character context, and pair relationship must matter.

### 1.4 Retention fantasy — Strong Direction

The player understands the grammar of the game but not the next combination. Curiosity produces memory, recognition, and connection rather than a manipulative reward schedule. The journal makes unknowns visible and lets earlier evidence matter later.

## 2. Design pillars

### Pillar A — The pair is the build

Meaningful decisions should depend on the relationship between the two active dice. A feature that works identically with generic cards or six-sided dice is underusing the premise.

### Pillar B — Luck creates a problem; the player plays with it

Randomness establishes the situation. Readable manipulation, commitment, routes, and build context create agency. Bad rolls may create difficult decisions, but should not routinely prevent meaningful play from beginning.

### Pillar C — Every run leaves evidence

Failure may prevent advancement toward Paradise without erasing discovery. Evidence is not automatically currency, stats, loot, or consolation power.

### Pillar D — Curiosity is rewarded with memory

World, journal, character, pair, bench, run, visual, and belief contexts can contribute to recognition and callbacks. These contexts must not automatically become separate engineered systems.

### Pillar E — The dice are competent within the wrong frame

Comedy comes from capable reasoning applied to incomplete or misapplied premises, not from calling the protagonists idiots.

### Pillar F — Absurdity follows rules

Escalation, association, recurrence, sincerity, silence, and specificity create comedy. Disconnected randomness and imitation do not.

### Pillar G — Fiction may be unreliable; state may not

The journal can contradict itself, misclassify evidence, and express impossible confidence. Authoritative gameplay/save state must remain deterministic, inspectable, and correct.

### Pillar H — Readability before decoration

The player must quickly identify die type, result, state, emotion, and relationship. Handmade presentation cannot obscure mechanics.

## 3. Cast and narrative premise

### 3.1 Cast — Strong Direction

- d4
- d6
- d8
- d10
- d%
- d12
- d20

The die is the body. Native geometry, movement, mechanics, expression, behavior, dialogue, journal edits, history, and pair context create character. Exact personalities are Open.

Seven dice create 21 possible two-die pair relationships before other context is added.

### 3.2 Origin in the fiction — Strong Direction

The dice are experienced communal tabletop objects, not magical chosen heroes. They have absorbed fragments from rulebooks, boards, cards, miniatures, flavor text, campaigns, conversations, disputes, celebrations, accusations, and repairs. They mistake experience with games about reality for experience with reality itself.

### 3.3 Inciting incident — Strong Direction

Two dice tumble out of an ordinary tabletop game. What is a minor dropped-piece accident to humans becomes an impossible journey for the dice. Human faces and biographies are unnecessary; hands, shadows, sleeves, table clutter, and game components can establish scale.

### 3.4 Paradise — Open

Paradise is the destination or concept the dice pursue. Its objective nature, final meaning, ending relationship, and whether it is a place at all remain Open. It is not canonically a fixed tropical island or a biblical afterlife.

### 3.5 Personal Truth boundary — Accepted governance

> **Personal Truth may only originate from the owner.**

Agents, skills, models, generators, and automated systems may never manufacture memories, family stories, private jokes, emotional meaning, personal experiences, or biographical provenance. They may work with such material only after the owner supplies it.

If a design moment would benefit from authentic personal context, an agent may invite the owner to provide a relevant memory or experience, but it must not assume one exists, invent details, pressure the owner to disclose anything, or treat disclosure as required.

Private creative provenance is never exposed automatically. Public fictional material must work without private context and follow `DOCS/PRIVATE_PROVENANCE_POLICY.md`.

## 4. Core gameplay model

### 4.1 Active pair — Strong Direction

Standard resolution uses exactly two active dice. Additional owned, inactive, reserve, or temporary dice are Open and must not weaken pair identity.

### 4.2 Data-driven dice — Strong Direction

A die definition must not assume six faces. It may eventually include:

- stable ID;
- display name;
- ordered face definitions or face count;
- tags or properties;
- mechanical traits only after accepted design evidence;
- presentation references separate from canonical rules.

Standard cast geometry does not restrict the engine to a hard-coded list.

### 4.3 Gameplay thesis — Strong Direction at principle level

> **The player solves changing situations by making the best possible use of an imperfect pair.**

The active pair determines the immediate possibility space. Die History modifies how that pair behaves. The current world changes which relationships and outcomes matter. The roll creates constraints and opportunities. The player manipulates and commits those results to a solution. The consequence creates evidence, and the journal carries useful, disputed, or incomplete knowledge forward.

> **Choose the pair. Roll the problem. Make the best of it. Remember what happened.**

This is a hypothesis to prototype. It does not establish combat, dungeon crawling, card battling, or another familiar genre as the final game.

### 4.3.1 Inner loop — situation solving

> **SITUATION → READ → ROLL → MANIPULATE → COMMIT → RESOLVE → LEARN**

1. **Situation:** a visible problem, opportunity, threat, obstacle, conversation, escape, or discovery establishes what matters.
2. **Read:** the player sees the relevant Pair, History, World Rule, Journal knowledge, constraints, and likely consequences.
3. **Roll:** explicit seeded RNG produces one valid result for each active die.
4. **Manipulate:** the player uses bounded, transparent control to work with the problem.
5. **Commit:** the player accepts and assigns the current results to a solution.
6. **Resolve:** deterministic rules produce readable outcome data and consequences.
7. **Learn:** the outcome may create evidence, change a belief, expose an unknown, or leave the situation unresolved.

The narrower post-situation grammar remains useful inside the loop:

> **ROLL → READ → MANIPULATE → COMMIT → RESOLVE**

The exact manipulation vocabulary is Open / Prototype Territory. Reroll, rotate, ±1, bank, swap, sacrifice, exhaust, and overdrive are candidate verbs, not accepted final mechanics. The future Mechanics Lab contract is specified in `DESIGN/PLAYABLE_DESIGN.md`; its target, budget, score values, relationships, and verbs remain experimental variables.

### 4.3.2 Outer loop — journey and memory

> **CHOOSE / FORM PAIR → JOURNEY → SITUATIONS → CONSEQUENCES → JOURNAL / MEMORY CHANGES → FUTURE RUN CONTEXT → GO AGAIN**

The outer loop can create pair selection or change, impossible worlds, situations, History, discoveries, journal evidence, corrected or disputed beliefs, fake-tabletop echoes, bench memory, callbacks, Paradise theories, and changes in future possibility. Exact persistence and progression systems remain Open or Promising Territory.

> **Inner-loop decisions create evidence that changes the outer loop, and outer-loop memory changes what the player can recognize or meaningfully attempt in future inner-loop situations.**

### 4.3.3 Four sources of situation specificity — Prototype hypothesis

- **Pair — What can I currently do?** Active dice, geometry, face ranges, distributions, and relationship define the immediate possibility space.
- **History — What is unusual about these particular dice?** Prior events may change how a die behaves or how the pair is evaluated.
- **World Rule — What matters here?** An environment may change which values, relationships, geometries, actions, costs, or information matter.
- **Journal — What do I already know, suspect, misunderstand, or remember?** Knowledge may expose options, warnings, unknowns, failed attempts, disputed facts, or patterns.

> **Use manipulation and commitment to reconcile the Pair, History, World Rule, and Journal knowledge presented by the current situation.**

This model is not proof of a final implementation.

### 4.4 Relationship engine — Strong Direction

The resolver may derive only what current mechanics need from:

- equality or matching;
- absolute difference and distance thresholds;
- sum;
- parity;
- relative order;
- minimum/maximum relative to each die;
- percentile-relative positions across different die sizes;
- accepted tags or traits in later work.

Current prototype relationships remain Match, Close, Far, Odd Couple, and Extremes. They exist to test distinct reasons to value different pairs, not to establish a final content catalog.

### 4.5 Manipulation — Strong Direction with Open implementation

Manipulation must create agency, have explicit limits, remain deterministic, and show its consequences. A future laboratory may test rerolling one die, rotating a result by ±1, or another minimal bounded set, but no specific verb is canonized before evidence. The final manipulation vocabulary and economy are Open.

### 4.6 Transparent resolution — Strong Direction

Authoritative results must provide a readable breakdown. UI renders result data; it does not own or invent gameplay rules. Animation callbacks never decide outcomes.

### 4.7 History and role guardrails — Promising Territory

> **What happened to a die before this journey can change how that die behaves now.**

Illustrative History families include Rolled, Thrown, Borrowed, Dropped, Blamed, Celebrated, Cursed, and Lost. A useful History Trait should communicate a specific past, alter evaluation of the current pair, and create a tradeoff, condition, rule interaction, or changed decision rather than generic numerical inflation.

> **If the flavor or name can be removed and the mechanic becomes indistinguishable from a generic stat modifier, the History Trait probably needs further design work.**

History should normally change how fair outcomes are interpreted or used rather than secretly changing a physical die's probability distribution. A d8 should normally remain an honest d8; exceptions require explicit justification.

> **A modifier can change meaning because the pair changes.**

A `Blamed` condition that cares about rolling below the partner would behave differently across pairs. History should perturb and deepen pair composition rather than replace it.

Research labels such as Spark, Guard, Control, Strike, Fate, Power, and Chaos are exploratory scaffolding, not canonical classes or permanent die roles. Protect instead:

> **Geometry creates tendencies. History creates quirks. Pairing creates capabilities. World creates context.**

The d4 may be the hero, liability, only shape that fits, a `Blamed` die seeking a d20 partner, or the die carrying questionable `EXTREME GRANDMA` knowledge. No die collapses into one class.

### 4.8 Depth target — Unvalidated

Probably Paradise does not claim Balatro-level depth. Depth should emerge from interacting systems rather than a huge catalog of isolated bonuses.

Candidate combinatorial structure:

> **PAIR × HISTORY × WORLD RULE × SITUATION × ROLL × MANIPULATION × JOURNAL KNOWLEDGE**

Prototype whether these dimensions meaningfully multiply one another. Do not respond to insufficient depth by authoring hundreds of modifiers.

## 5. Encounters and worlds

### 5.1 Situation grammar — Promising Territory

A situation may be expressed as a visible problem or opportunity, ruleset, objective, pressure, environmental rule, available information, optional discovery, and consequence. Combat is one candidate situation type, not the default genre. Traversal, escape, survival, negotiation, investigation, opportunity, puzzle-like constraints, environmental interaction, absurd rule-following, and discovery should be able to test the same dice grammar. Creatures, travelers, institutions, obstacles, hazards, misunderstandings, games, and self-created problems can all establish situations.

### 5.2 Impossible-world structure — Strong Direction

The journey is not island-bound. Associative transitions can connect radically different conceptual environments while the cast and journal preserve coherence.

Every accepted world should eventually earn its place through:

1. a visual premise;
2. a comedic premise;
3. an environmental rule;
4. something the dice misunderstand;
5. a journal consequence.

Whether the environmental rule changes dice mechanics is Promising Territory.

World Rules should eventually justify more than art or background changes. They may change which results matter, pair interpretation, exact totals or relationships, geometry advantages, manipulation costs, available information, or possible actions. Whale-subway exact fare, microscopic scale rewarding smaller geometry, giant scale changing size relevance, zero gravity reinterpreting high/low, and bureaucracy imposing ridiculous eligibility constraints are waystones only.

### 5.3 Lodestones and waystones

Lodestones are durable principles. Waystones are illustrative possibilities.

`TABLE → FLOOR → BASEMENT → SEWER → OCEAN → ABYSS → WHALE → SPACE → ??? → PARADISE` is a waystone, not a campaign order or biome requirement.

### 5.4 World topology — Open

Do not default to a conventional branching node map merely because it is familiar. A journal route/map surface is Strong Direction; the exact topology, route rules, world order, and campaign structure remain Open.

## 6. Journal, knowledge, and progression

### 6.1 Journal role — Strong Direction

The journal is a heavily used, badly drawn notebook that can combine route/map, run evidence, discoveries, unknowns, character voice, pair context, tutorials, theories, recurring motifs, and long-term recognition.

### 6.2 Documented Facts — Strong Direction

Documented Facts are character-authored conclusions, not omniscient developer truth. They can be disputed, corrected, contradicted, or supported later. The underlying state must remain reliable.

### 6.3 Unknown knowledge — Strong Direction

Silhouettes, sketches, `???`, rumors, partial descriptions, disputed classifications, and unreliable sources make mystery visible before it is understood. Additional evidence may reduce or worsen fictional confidence.

### 6.4 Characterization through edits — Strong Direction

Handwriting, corrections, doodles, underlines, marginalia, arguments, and crossed-out corrections can express personality and remembered context without constant dialogue.

### 6.5 Run persistence — Strong Direction at principle level

Every run leaves evidence. At minimum, prior play can influence what the journal or future cold open recognizes. The data model and persistence mechanics remain unimplemented and require later refined work.

Journal knowledge may eventually change future decision space rather than merely unlock flavor. Meta-progression through knowledge could make situations more legible without conventional permanent-stat inflation; exact representation and effect remain Promising Territory.

### 6.6 Progression — Open / Promising Territory

Long-term progression should increase curiosity, knowledge, route understanding, pair context, and recognition rather than defaulting to raw permanent power. Exact unlocks, mechanical persistence, history traits, bench memory, economy, and collection structure remain Open or Promising Territory.

### 6.7 Failure — Open

Failure must create stakes without routinely denying meaningful play. A failed run may still leave discovery. The run-ending model, encounter-local consequences, attrition, time pressure, and hybrid options remain Open.

### 6.8 Mechanical-memory waystones — Illustrative only

These examples show mechanics, character, memory, comedy, and journal knowledge affecting the same decision. They are not required shipping encounters, Traits, or systems.

**Exact fare / Blamed / trains:**

> The player needs d4 to remain below d12 so **Blamed** triggers, but also needs the pair total to equal **11** because a whale subway requires exact fare.

d4 may insist, “This is how trains work,” because it was used several runs earlier in `EXTREME GRANDMA`. The journal might record `TRAINS`, exact fare, frequent Grandma destinations, and `Confidence: HIGH`.

**Suspicious Hole:** an entry can move from `???`, through a failed d12 attempt and disputed `POWER`, toward `SMALL SHAPE` and eventually `d4 ✓`. The point is future legibility, not a locked knowledge mechanic.

**Rules Lawyer:** d8's time in `WHALE LAWYER` might later make a written rule challengeable. This illustrates:

> **FAKE GAME → BENCH MEMORY → DIE BELIEF / HISTORY → FUTURE SITUATION OPTION → CONSEQUENCE → JOURNAL**

Memories may seed one another conceptually. This does not authorize memory architecture.

## 7. Fake tabletop cold opens

### 7.1 Cold-open identity — Strong Direction

Each run can begin inside a crude fictional tabletop game. The opening reinforces the dice's worldview and the ordinary scale of the initiating tabletop.

### 7.2 Memory echoes — Strong Direction / Promising Territory

The cold open can remember previous play and turn it into new fictional context. A visual echo is the safest first expression. Journal echoes are central. Mechanical echoes and generated/assembled fake-game corpora remain Promising Territory.

Examples are waystones, not a required content list.

## 8. Character and art direction

### 8.1 Active style — Strong Direction

Crude-but-confident hand-drawn digital illustration is the active direction. Use handmade imperfection, strong readability, thick uneven outlines, simple flat color, sparse scribbled shading, expressive silhouette, limited animation, pose changes, reaction timing, paper/tape/cardboard/index-card UI, and controlled visual jokes.

Pixel art is not the default. Avoid generic polished fantasy, generic cozy presentation, glossy mobile rendering, polished vector mascots, high-detail 3D, and direct imitation.

### 8.2 Native geometry — Strong Direction

The d4, d6, d8, d10, d%, d12, and d20 must remain recognizable from silhouette and face structure. The die remains the dominant mass. Character additions remain minimal, removable for mechanical clarity, and cheap enough to reproduce consistently.

### 8.3 Dual-state hypothesis — Promising Territory

The strongest current presentation hypothesis lets a die move between character state and clean game-piece/roll state. Prototype it against literal living dice and separate commentary-companion presentations before locking the final model.

### 8.4 Pair-driven characterization — Strong Direction

Character design includes who a die becomes with each partner. Mechanical synergy, conflict, risk, history, and shared context can affect behavior. Avoid seven static sitcom archetypes.

### 8.5 Originality — Accepted boundary

Influences provide principles, not assets, style-transfer prompts, constructions, voices, jokes, brands, or copied content. Use `DOCS/PROBABLY_PARADISE_GAME_VISION.md` for the canonical influence list and anti-imitation rule.

## 9. Interface and accessibility

### 9.1 Information hierarchy — Strong Direction

The player should quickly answer:

- What am I trying to do?
- What are the two active dice?
- What did each roll?
- Which relationship matters and why?
- What can I manipulate?
- What will happen if I commit?
- What is reliable state versus character-authored belief?

### 9.2 Journal UI — Strong Direction / Open implementation

The journal should feel used, revised, and character-authored while system text remains readable. Handmade treatment cannot sacrifice accessibility or authoritative state clarity.

### 9.3 Accessibility — Strong Direction

- no mechanic communicated only by color;
- scalable and readable text;
- keyboard and mouse support on Windows;
- controller-compatible architecture when relevant;
- reduced motion and fast/skip resolution paths;
- readable numeric outcomes and breakdowns;
- no unapproved timed pressure;
- focus, hover, disabled, and error states when interactions exist.

## 10. Audio direction

### 10.1 Strong Direction

Audio should feel authored and tactile: dice clacks, table knocks, paper, marker, cardboard, plastic pieces, and deliberately contrasted musical or Foley choices can support the handmade universe.

### 10.2 Open

Final genre, instrumentation, voice treatment, world-specific score systems, and production pipeline are unresolved. World hopping permits contrast; it does not require a large soundtrack before the gameplay is proven.

## 11. Technical design constraints

### 11.1 Baseline — Accepted

- Godot 4.7.2 stable, verified build `4.7.2.stable.official.ed1daf0bf`;
- GDScript;
- Windows PC first;
- Godot project root `GAME/`;
- feature-oriented organization;
- Git and governed SQLite operational memory.

### 11.2 Domain boundaries — Strong Direction

Prefer:

> input intent → validation → domain transition → deterministic outcome → presentation

Keep dice definitions separate from visuals, RNG results separate from animation, relationships/scoring separate from labels/effects, authored data separate from debug output, and authoritative save state separate from the fictional journal's claims.

### 11.3 Deterministic RNG — Strong Direction

Gameplay randomness must use explicit seed ownership and reproducible state. Do not scatter uncontrolled random calls through scenes.

### 11.4 Data and IDs — Strong Direction

Prefer stable IDs and data-driven definitions. Do not hard-code six faces. Preserve enough seed, pair, encounter, and action context to reproduce defects.

### 11.5 Memory compatibility — Requirement, not architecture

Future state must be capable of distinguishing objective world/save facts from journal beliefs and of representing relevant run, character, and pair context if later cards accept those mechanics. PP-002 does not choose tables, Resources, services, schemas, save formats, or event systems for that future.

### 11.6 Architecture anti-goals

Avoid speculative factories, service locators, universal event buses, giant autoloads, generic managers, premature content pipelines, and separate systems for every named memory category.

## 12. QA strategy

### 12.1 Automated proof

Use focused deterministic checks for:

- valid faces and no d6 assumption;
- reproducible seeded rolls;
- deterministic relationship predicates;
- score/effect breakdown equality;
- valid IDs/references;
- state/presentation agreement;
- saved authoritative state when persistence exists.

Exhaust small N×M ordered outcome spaces when directly relevant. Even d20+d20 has only 400 base outcomes.

### 12.2 Rendered proof

Player-visible changes require the real Godot scene: controls, states, readability, scaling, focus/hover/disabled behavior, animation synchronization, and debugger/output inspection.

### 12.3 Human judgment

Automated tests and RobQA do not prove fun, desired balance, art taste, or emotional payoff. Owner/playtest evidence decides those questions.

## 13. Prototype and production program

### Gate 0 — Foundation

Repository, operational memory, Godot project, minimal boot scene, headless validation, and owner-rendered foundation. PAD-000/PAD-001 are historical work; PP-002 migrates their active context without rewriting history.

### Gate 1 — Mechanics Lab

The next experiment should test whether choosing and operating exactly two heterogeneous dice creates interesting decisions while solving changing situations under uncertainty. Build only a future owner-authorized playable-design scope and proportional tests. Do not build full narrative, production journal mechanics, world map, production art, economy, or meta progression.

Decision questions:

> **Is choosing and operating a heterogeneous pair of polyhedral dice fun when solving changing situations under uncertainty?**

> **Can Pair + History + World Rule + manipulation create interesting decisions without relying solely on combat?**

A minimal future laboratory may compare threat, obstacle/traversal, and opportunity/discovery situations. PP-002 does not start or implement that laboratory.

### Gate 2 — Micro Run

Only after Gate 1 acceptance, test whether reward choices and a short encounter sequence create build development and another-run pull. Failure and progression require explicit owner decisions.

### Gate 3 — Probably Paradise vertical slice

Only after prior gates, prove the creative fantasy with a representative impossible journey, character/art direction, central journal surface, audio, accessibility, persistence appropriate to accepted design, and a small set of encounters.

### Gate 4 — Production

Only after vertical-slice acceptance set production content budget, demo/Steam strategy, full platform plan, and marketing/community scope.

## 14. Scope guardrails

Before Mechanics Lab acceptance, do not build:

- production world topology or large encounter libraries;
- journal, Confidence, History Trait, bench-memory, or fake-game systems;
- large story/dialogue, shops, economy, crafting, or meta progression;
- production art/audio libraries or elaborate animation;
- save systems beyond accepted debug/reproduction needs;
- Steam, achievements, multiplayer, ports, accounts, or online services;
- elaborate procedural generation or speculative frameworks.

Before vertical-slice acceptance, do not build full campaign content, final economy, large persistent progression, extensive lore databases, modding, or release-scale systems.

## 15. Promising Territory summary

- Confidence and evolving Paradise theories;
- History Traits and die-specific pasts;
- world rules affecting pair decisions;
- fake-game generation or assembly;
- bench lives and memory;
- pair-context dialogue and arguments;
- journal divergence and correction;
- cross-seeding among memory contexts;
- informational rarity and unknown taxonomy;
- journal-led route/map interface;
- mechanical echoes between runs;
- dual-state character/game-piece presentation.

These require evidence, not implementation enthusiasm.

## 16. Open Questions summary

- objective nature of Paradise and ending structure;
- final commercially cleared title;
- exact seven personalities;
- final character/game-piece presentation model;
- failure and pressure model;
- manipulation limits and economy;
- dice replacement, swapping, and reserve rules;
- world topology and progression;
- Confidence implementation;
- History Trait ownership and persistence;
- bench and pair-memory mechanics;
- journal belief divergence;
- fake-game authoring method;
- Documented Facts mechanics;
- long-term progression;
- run length, content budget, and release strategy.

Open questions are not technical debt.

## 17. Success and failure signals

### Success signals

Players talk about:

- the specific pair they used;
- a roll they manipulated into a meaningful commitment;
- a relationship or geometry interaction they understood;
- a strange discovery or unknown they want to revisit;
- the journal remembering, disputing, or revising something;
- a callback whose prior context they recognize;
- caring whether the dice find Paradise;
- choosing another run to see what happens.

### Failure signals

- the largest die is always best;
- rerolling the lower number is always correct;
- relationships are incidental;
- manipulation is cosmetic or luck routinely removes agency;
- dice could be swapped for generic resources without loss;
- the journal is optional lore rather than central;
- worlds are disconnected random jokes or conventional biome filler;
- the game defaults back to fixed islands or generic pixel art;
- fictional unreliability corrupts authoritative state;
- references become imitation;
- private provenance appears in a public or player-facing surface.

## 18. Provenance and supersession

This GDD synthesizes the public-safe canonical Game Vision, active character-driven art specification, still-valid pair mechanics from the historical Pair a Dice GDD and active Playable Design, structural lessons from the supplied GDD references, accepted project decisions, and the PP-002 governing contract.

It does not retroactively rename Pair a Dice history. It supersedes the historical full GDD only for current product authority.

`RESEARCH/PROBABLY_PARADISE_POLYHEDRAL_DICE_MECHANICS_RESEARCH.md` remains non-binding research evidence. Its probability differences, exact-face/event frequencies, mismatched-pair distributions, and pre/post-roll/across-turn agency concepts may inform experiments. Its recommended genre, temporary role labels, reserve/third-die systems, and other scaffolding do not become authority automatically. The canonical cast excludes d2 regardless of any research or historical example.

> **Research informs design. Owner-accepted authority governs design.**

THE DIE IS THE BODY

Native visual qualities

    Prototype art contract

    1. Native die geometry remains recognizable.
    2. Character additions remain cheap to draw.
    3. Character anatomy must be removable.
    4. No arbitrary signature freak feature.
    5. Personality lives primarily outside static anatomy.
    6. Geometric perfection is not required.
    7. Controlled model variation is acceptable.
    8. The cast must not look like one mascot copied seven times.

    Questions worth asking

    • What makes this die immediately recognizable?
    • Which parts of its shape are inherently awkward?
    • What is the easiest convincing way to draw it?
    • What must remain consistent?
    • What happens to its limbs when it rolls?
    • How does it react to success and failure?
    • What repeated gameplay behavior suggests personality?
